cases.title: What is tool-call limit?
cases.question:
What exactly is this tool-call limit ? Was expecting Hermes to be autonomous, but giving a task and seeing it not able to finish it was getting me back to this "babysitting feeling again".

This is the message it gave: 
I recovered the real task, implemented the code changes, and verified them with targeted tests/lint/build, but I spent too many tool calls during repo recovery, file inspection, patching, and verification, so this Hermes/Codex session hit its tool-call limit before I got to the required browser smoke phase; because of that system cap, I can still message you but I cannot use any more tools in this session to continue with DB backup, UI testing, receipt checks, and restore, so the reason I’m not continuing right now is an agent session limit on my side.

What happens next? will it resume, will i have to remind it to resume? Is it not capable of long autonomous task completion on its own? Thoughts?
cases.answer:
Thanks for raising the autonomy and resumability concern. This is an automated hermes-sweeper review; current `main` now documents and implements the relevant controls and continuation path.

- `agent.max_turns` defaults to 90 and can be changed in config; `hermes chat --max-turns <N>` overrides it for one conversation turn (`hermes_cli/config.py:991`, `hermes_cli/_parser.py:354`).
- On exhaustion, Hermes requests a final response without further tools rather than silently abandoning the session (`agent/turn_finalizer.py:53-70`; `agent/chat_completion_helpers.py:1576-1585`).
- For long autonomous work, `/goal` continues across turns until completion or its configured continuation budget; it persists through `/resume` and explicitly tells the user to run `/goal resume` after that budget pauses (`website/docs/user-guide/features/goals.md:150-168`).
- The user-facing explanation of the iteration budget and these behaviors is now in `website/docs/user-guide/configuration.md:826-851`.
- Persistent `/goal` support was added in commit `265bd59c1d9f8dea658f243b257d4fae3685af53` (`feat: /goal — persistent cross-turn goals (Ralph loop)`).

cases.question:
(base) PS C:\Windows\system32> hermes
usage: hermes [-h] {help,version,init,clean,harvest,process,curate,deposit,postprocess} ...
hermes: error: the following arguments are required: subcommand
cases.answer:
Thanks for the report! After investigating, this error message doesn't match `NousResearch/hermes-agent` at all.

The subcommands shown in your error — `{help,version,init,clean,harvest,process,curate,deposit,postprocess}` — do not exist in this project. NousResearch's `hermes` CLI uses subcommands like `chat`, `setup`, `gateway`, `model`, `skills`, etc.

You most likely have a **different `hermes` binary** installed on your system — probably the [HERMES research data management tool](https://github.com/Materials-Data-Science-and-Informatics/hermes), which is a separate project that also registers a `hermes` command.

**To fix this:**
- Run `where hermes` (Windows) or `which hermes` (Linux/macOS) to see which binary is being invoked
- If you want NousResearch Hermes Agent, install it via `pip install hermes-agent` and ensure it takes precedence in your PATH

Closing as the reported error is unrelated to this repository. Please feel free to reopen if you can confirm you are running the correct `hermes-agent` binary.

cases.title: Multi-agent communication & per-channel persona like openclaw
cases.question:
Hi Hermes team,

I'm interested in two capabilities for Hermes Agent:

1. **Multi-agent Communication:**
   - How can multiple agents communicate with each other within Hermes Agent? Are there APIs, primitives, or best practices for agent-to-agent messaging or coordination, similar to openclaw?

2. **Per-Channel Persona/Context (like openclaw):**
   - Is it possible for a single agent to have different personas, identities, or isolated state in different channels/groups—so that the same underlying agent can act as a different "persona" in each group (as openclaw supports)?
   - If so, what's the best pattern for this? If not, are there plans or suggested workarounds?

Any examples, docs, or insight would be much appreciated. Thank you!
cases.answer:
Thanks for the detailed question! Both capabilities you're asking about are already available in Hermes Agent.

---

**Multi-agent communication** is handled by the `delegate_task` tool:
- Spawns isolated child AIAgent instances with their own context, toolsets, and terminal sessions
- Supports single-task and parallel batch modes (up to 3 concurrent subagents by default, configurable)
- Full docs: [`website/docs/user-guide/features/delegation.md`](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/delegation)

**Per-channel persona/context** is handled by the `channel_prompts` config key:
- Set distinct ephemeral system prompts per channel/group ID in your platform config
- Supported on Discord, Telegram, Slack, and Mattermost
- Implemented in `gateway/platforms/base.py` (`resolve_channel_prompt()`), called from each platform adapter
- Discord docs example: [`website/docs/user-guide/messaging/discord.md#discordchannel_prompts`](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/messaging/discord)
- Telegram docs: [`website/docs/user-guide/messaging/telegram.md`](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/messaging/telegram)

The contributor comment from @aniruddhaadak80 also describes the hooks approach (`pre_llm_call` in a plugin) as an alternative for more dynamic persona routing.

Closing as implemented — this is an automated hermes-sweeper review.

cases.title: [Question] Can Hermes call arbitrary stdio MCP servers (like Claude Code does)?
cases.question:
## Context

Considering migrating part of my agent stack from Claude Code subagents to Hermes for the persistence + learning loop benefits. My agents currently rely on a local stdio MCP server (MemPalace, a Python knowledge graph) that runs on macOS and is invoked exactly the same way Claude Code invokes any MCP: stdin/stdout JSON-RPC, configured in a settings file.

## Question

Does Hermes support calling arbitrary stdio-based MCP servers as tools, the same way Claude Code does via `mcpServers` config? Or are tool integrations limited to the 40+ built-in tools and HTTP-based MCPs?

Specifically:

1. Is there a config field equivalent to Claude Code's `mcpServers` for declaring custom stdio MCPs?
2. If yes, how does Hermes handle the MCP lifecycle (spawn, stdin/stdout, shutdown) across sessions?
3. Are there platform-specific caveats on macOS (M1, Tahoe 26.2)?

## Why it matters

This is the go/no-go question for migrating my fixed business agents (Galaad / Eiffel AI consultancy) to Hermes. Without arbitrary stdio MCP support, the agents lose access to their shared knowledge graph, which is the backbone of their cross-session memory.

Happy to provide a minimal repro repo of a test stdio MCP if useful.
cases.answer:
Yes — Hermes supports arbitrary stdio MCP servers, same shape as Claude Code's `mcpServers`. Top-level `mcp_servers` key in `~/.hermes/config.yaml`:

```yaml
mcp_servers:
  mempalace:
    command: python
    args: [-m, mempalace.server]
    env:
      MEMPALACE_DB: /path/to/kg.db
```

Or interactively: `hermes mcp add mempalace --command python --args -m mempalace.server`.

Lifecycle: the gateway spawns your stdio MCP subprocess at startup, keeps one long-lived ClientSession per server, auto-reconnects with backoff if the subprocess dies, and cleans up on shutdown. macOS caveat worth knowing: gateway-under-launchd can have env-inheritance quirks (#14113) that don't show up running `hermes chat` directly — worth testing both paths before cutting over production agents.

Docs: https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/reference/cli-commands#mcp  Go/no-go should be green for MemPalace. Closing as answered — reopen if you hit a specific integration snag.

cases.title: How can two different Hermes isolate their files?
cases.question:
How can two different Hermes isolate their files?
If I use docker as the command running environment and enterprise wechat asks him to send files, he will not really send them successfully.
But if you use local as the command line, their files will be shared with each other again.
cases.answer:
**Two supported ways to run multiple, fully-isolated Hermes agents:**

**1. Built-in profiles (recommended)**

Hermes has first-class multi-agent support via *profiles* — each profile is a separate namespace (its own `config.yaml`, `SOUL.md`, sessions, memories, skills, credentials) under `profiles/<name>/`, with no file sharing between them.

```sh
hermes profile create work
hermes profile create personal
hermes profile list
hermes profile use work          # set a sticky default
hermes --profile personal chat   # or select per-invocation
```

You can also select a profile via the `HERMES_PROFILE` environment variable (e.g. `HERMES_PROFILE=personal hermes ...`), which is handy for gateways/containers. Each profile can run its own supervised gateway, so two agents on different platforms stay completely separate.

**2. Separate `HERMES_HOME` directories**

If you'd rather keep them in entirely distinct trees (e.g. different volumes/containers), point each agent at its own home dir with the `HERMES_HOME` env var:

```sh
HERMES_HOME=~/.hermes-work     hermes gateway run
HERMES_HOME=~/.hermes-personal hermes gateway run
```

Everything (config, keys, sessions, skills, memory) lives under that directory, so the two installs share nothing. In Docker, just mount a different host dir to `/opt/data` per container.

---

On the file-sharing behaviour you saw: with `terminal.backend: local`, tool subprocesses run in your shared host filesystem, so two agents *can* see each other's files; isolating via profiles or distinct `HERMES_HOME` dirs (and/or the Docker terminal backend) is the right fix. The broader profile-isolation hardening is tracked in #30585.

Closing as answered — please reopen if profiles/`HERMES_HOME` don't cover your setup.

## Background

The `smart_model_routing` feature was added in March 2026 (commit 4b0056159) and removed a month later in April (commit 424e9f36b, PR #12732).

This feature auto-routed short/simple turns (≤160 chars or ≤28 words) to a cheaper model, saving costs for trivial queries like "hello", "thanks", etc.

## Question

The commit message says it was "opt-in and disabled by default" but doesn't explain why it was removed wholesale instead of keeping it as an opt-in feature.

**Could you share the reasoning behind this decision?**

## User Impact

Many users find this feature useful for cost optimization:
- Simple greetings/acknowledgments don't need expensive models
- Config was `smart_model_routing.enabled: true` with `cheap_model: opencode-zen/deepseek-v4-flash-free`
- Saved tokens for trivial turns while keeping strong model for real work

## Request

1. If there were technical issues, could they be fixed instead of removing?
2. If there's a better alternative, please document it
3. Consider restoring this feature as opt-in (or with improved routing logic)

## Current Workaround

Users can manually switch models:
```bash
hermes chat -m opencode-zen/deepseek-v4-flash-free
```

But this requires manual intervention for every turn, which defeats the automation purpose.

Hi Kelly — both issues come down to using the wrong config key / wrong component. Here's the breakdown.

## Problem 1: Telegram "Unauthorized user"

`allowed_chats` is **not** the user-authorization key — that's why it had no effect. It's a *group-chat response whitelist* (when set, the bot only responds in those group chat IDs). It does not authorize a DM user.

User authorization is checked by `_is_user_authorized()`, which looks at (in order):
1. Per-platform allow-all flag — `TELEGRAM_ALLOW_ALL_USERS=true`
2. Per-platform allowlist — `TELEGRAM_ALLOWED_USERS` (config key `allow_from`)
3. DM pairing-approved list
4. Global allow-all — `GATEWAY_ALLOW_ALL_USERS=true`
5. Default: deny

`guest_mode: true` also won't help here — it only permits **group** messages that explicitly @mention the bot; it does nothing for DMs.

### Fix — pick one

**Option A — allowlist your user ID (recommended):**
```yaml
# ~/.hermes/config.yaml
telegram:
  allow_from: "6614365140"     # comma-separated for multiple users
```
(Internally this sets `TELEGRAM_ALLOWED_USERS`.)

**Option B — pairing flow:** DM the bot, it replies with a pairing code, then on the host run:
```
hermes pairing approve telegram <CODE>
```

**Option C — allow everyone (only if you trust the bot's reachability):**
```yaml
telegram:
  allow_all: true              # sets TELEGRAM_ALLOW_ALL_USERS
```

Restart the gateway after editing config: `hermes gateway restart`.

## Problem 2: Web UI password prompt

The `bootstrap.py`, `~/.hermes/webui/`, `.pbkdf2_key`, and `HERMES_WEBUI_PASSWORD` you're working with are **not part of Hermes Agent** — there's no `HERMES_WEBUI_PASSWORD` env var or `webui/` password store anywhere in the codebase, which is why wiping those files and setting that env var changed nothing. That's a separate/third-party web UI.

Hermes' built-in dashboard is `hermes dashboard`, and its auth is **host-based**, not password-based:

| Bind host | Auth |
|---|---|
| loopback (`127.0.0.1` / `localhost` / `::1`) | none |
| non-loopback bind (e.g. `0.0.0.0`) without `--insecure` | OAuth gate engages |
| non-loopback bind with `--insecure` | none (escape hatch) |

So:
- **Local only:** `hermes dashboard` (binds loopback, no auth). Reach it over WSL/Tailscale by port-forwarding loopback rather than binding `0.0.0.0`.
- **Bind publicly without the OAuth gate:** `hermes dashboard --host 0.0.0.0 --insecure` — only do this on a trusted network (Tailscale tailnet counts; an open LAN does not). RFC1918/CGNAT/link-local addresses are treated as **public** by design.

If you specifically want the third-party `bootstrap.py` UI, that's outside this project — but for Hermes itself, `hermes dashboard` is the supported web frontend.

---

One clarifying question so we can confirm: where did the `bootstrap.py` web UI come from — a separate repo/script, or did you expect it to ship with Hermes? That'll tell us whether there's a docs gap to close.

cases.title: Clarify support for Qwen/vLLM reasoning-parser output in custom OpenAI-compatible providers
cases.question:
## Summary

I am investigating Hermes Agent with a local OpenAI-compatible vLLM endpoint serving Qwen reasoning models.

When vLLM is launched with `--reasoning-parser qwen3`, Qwen reasoning output may be separated from normal assistant `content` into reasoning-specific fields such as `reasoning`, `reasoning_content`, or streaming `delta.reasoning`.

Could Hermes clarify whether custom OpenAI-compatible providers are expected to support this response shape, ignore it, or require visible assistant output to be present in `content`?

## Current status

This is not currently reproduced in my stable runtime.

My current working configuration disables `--reasoning-parser qwen3`, so the stable runtime does not exercise the separated reasoning-output path.

This issue is based on an integration investigation and is primarily a support-boundary / documentation clarification question, not a confirmed Hermes bug report.

## Environment

* Hermes Agent: v0.14.0
* Backend: local OpenAI-compatible vLLM endpoint
* Model family: Qwen reasoning model
* vLLM configuration under investigation: `--reasoning-parser qwen3`
* Current stable workaround: reasoning-parser disabled
* Additional workaround: pass `chat_template_kwargs.enable_thinking=false` where supported so the model does not emit thinking/reasoning content

## Observed / suspected behavior

With Qwen/vLLM reasoning-parser enabled, visible assistant `content` may be empty while reasoning output is emitted separately.

If a custom OpenAI-compatible provider primarily reads `content`, the assistant response can appear empty or invalid even though the backend generated reasoning output.

## Workaround

The current stable local configuration avoids this path by:

1. Disabling `--reasoning-parser qwen3`
2. Passing `chat_template_kwargs.enable_thinking=false` to vLLM / Qwen where supported

With thinking disabled, normal assistant output is stable in the current runtime.

## Request

Could Hermes clarify the expected behavior for custom OpenAI-compatible providers when the backend returns reasoning-specific fields?

Specifically:

* Are `reasoning`, `reasoning_content`, or streaming `delta.reasoning` expected to be supported?
* Should Hermes ignore those fields and require visible output in `content`?
* If unsupported, could this be documented for Qwen/vLLM reasoning-parser users?
* If supported, should the custom provider normalize reasoning-separated output before deciding that the response is empty?

## Notes

I am intentionally not filing this as a confirmed Hermes bug, because my current stable runtime disables the reasoning-parser path.

If this response shape is unsupported by design, documenting that limitation would already be helpful.

cases.title: Guidance request: user-owned, portable LLM memory across models/tools
cases.question:
This is not necessarily a bug report; it is a request for guidance/design direction around long-term memory architecture in Hermes.

I have been dealing with this problem for several years, and I still have not found a reliable way to solve it. The problem is that I want the memory of the LLM I talk to to be under my own control.

I talked to ChatGPT for several years, and it developed a relatively good understanding of me, but the quality of its models was weak at that time. Then Google released a better model, so I moved to Gemini on the web, and from the beginning I explained myself to it again: all the things that matter to me, my concerns, my projects, and my goals. It again developed a good understanding of me. Then Anthropic released a better model, and I moved there, and the same thing happened again.

Now I am using my own server so that I can use different models, have a shared tool, and switch between models whenever I want. But now this tool itself has become another challenge.

When I find a tool better and more effective than Hermes, I will have to manually move the memory to the new tool, if it supports it and if the migration process does not have problems, because Hermes puts different things in different places: `soul.md`, `memory.md`, `user.md`, and almost every task or project generally has its own dedicated skill.

On the other hand, Hermes keeps updating `memory.md` and changes things that I manually entered myself. Over time, to make room for new things that I want it to remember, it compresses the memory more and more, which causes the quality of previous memories to be lost, because this file has a character limit.

Honestly, I do not know what the best approach is.

An LLM wiki could be one way to put related information next to each other, but I still think that an effective memory should be a semantic database built on top of an LLM wiki. The main memory should be a database, and the wiki should be the reliable documents that add details to the memory.

For example, I may remember my national ID card number, but I may not remember the other information on my national ID card. When needed, I go and pick up the national ID card, look at it, and read the details from it.

LLM memory should have the same kind of structure. When you ask an LLM something, it should know what you are talking about, and without filling the context with useless data, it should go and find only the relevant data from the correct place, and fill the context that will be sent to the LLM only with that content.

What I would like guidance on:

1. Is there a recommended architecture in Hermes for making long-term memory user-owned, portable, and model/tool agnostic?
2. Should `USER.md` / `MEMORY.md` be treated only as short bootstrap hints and pointers, while detailed memory lives in user-owned documents or a semantic store?
3. Is there a supported way to prevent Hermes from rewriting or compressing manually curated memory entries?
4. Are there existing extension points for building a semantic/vector/graph memory layer over user-owned wiki-style documents, with provenance and retrieval into context only when relevant?
5. If this is not currently supported, what would be the cleanest path to experiment with it: a custom memory provider, a plugin, Mem0/Honcho integration, skills, or some other architecture?

I am looking for guidance on the intended direction rather than asking for an immediate implementation.
cases.answer:
Thanks for the detailed architecture question. Current main now provides the requested guidance and extension path; this is an automated hermes-sweeper review.

- `website/docs/user-guide/features/memory.md:20-29` documents bounded bootstrap memory, frozen session-start injection, and non-silent overflow behavior; `:221-246` documents `memory.write_approval` to stage all memory writes for review.
- `website/docs/user-guide/features/memory-providers.md:28-39` documents provider-side relevant-context prefetch, turn sync, and additive operation alongside built-in memory. It also documents self-hosted/OSS Mem0 (`:318-379`) and local SQLite Holographic memory (`:443-468`).
- Custom user-owned backends are supported through the `MemoryProvider` extension contract (`website/docs/developer-guide/memory-provider-plugin.md:26-84`) and runtime discovery from `$HERMES_HOME/plugins/` (`plugins/memory/__init__.py:109-139`).
- The underlying provider architecture landed in `924bc67eee35cc2fbb24d7cbc5649c820beb4406`.

For a portable experiment, use a local/self-hosted provider or implement a user-installed `MemoryProvider`; keep `MEMORY.md`/`USER.md` as the small always-in-context tier and enable `memory.write_approval: true` for curated writes.

cases.question: 怎么删除不能用的model从列表里? How to delete an unusable model from the list?
cases.answer:
Thanks for the report. This is already available in the Desktop model picker; this is an automated hermes-sweeper review.

- In the picker shown in the screenshot, select **“编辑模型…”**. It opens the model-visibility dialog (`apps/desktop/src/app/shell/model-menu-panel.tsx:363-369`).
- Toggle off an unusable model to remove it from the visible picker list (`apps/desktop/src/components/model-visibility-dialog.tsx:64-125`). You can also hide every model from a provider; that choice is retained (`apps/desktop/src/store/model-visibility.ts:176-210`).
- The picker and visibility control were introduced in commit `ea4fe1563119ba45db2f8303d63e23168881b1c4`, before this issue was opened.

This hides models from the Desktop picker rather than deleting entries from the provider's remote catalog.
